topics.title: 50th Anniversary of Skikkim’s Intergration
bullets: Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Sikkim on April 27-28, 2026, to participate in the closing ceremony of the state’s 50th year of Statehood celebrations in Gangtok.
During the visit, he inaugurated a comprehensive development package exceeding Rs 4,000 crore, aimed at strengthening infrastructure and promoting inclusive growth across sectors.
The Prime Minister also visited the Orchidarium in Gangtok, developed as a world-class Orchid Experience Centre to showcase the state’s rich ecological and floral heritage. History –
The kingdom of Sikkim was established in 1642 when three Tibetan lamas consecrated Phuntsong Namgyal as the first Chogyal (king), beginning a royal line that lasted 333 years.
The Namgyal dynasty ruled as a hereditary monarchy, with the Chogyals governing the strategically located Himalayan territory sandwiched between India, China, Nepal and Bhutan.
The last Chogyal, Palden Thondup Namgyal, was in power when the monarchy was finally abolished through a referendum in 1975.
On February 10, 1817, the British East India Company signed the Treaty of Titaliya with the Chogyal of Sikkim, returning Sikkimese land annexed by Nepal and guaranteeing British protection.
The treaty gave the British authorities significant commercial and political advantages in the region and established a friendly alliance against the expansionist Gurkha kingdom.
This agreement also set the stage for future British intervention, eventually leading to the 1835 gift of Darjeeling to the British East India Company.
The Treaty of Tumlong (March 1861) was signed after two British military expeditions (1850 and 1861), formally establishing Sikkim as a British protectorate.
Under Article 8, all restrictions on travel and trade by British subjects were abolished, and the British were permitted to intervene in the internal affairs of the country.
The treaty also imposed a Rs. 7,000 indemnity on Sikkim for "instigating" the British invasion, cementing British paramountcy in the region.
The Calcutta Convention of 1890, signed by Viceroy Lord Lansdowne and Qing China, formally demarcated the border between Sikkim and Tibet.
The convention recognized British protection over Sikkim and ceded a large tract of territory to Britain, influencing the modern-day Doklam border dispute.
The Lhasa Convention of 1904 affirmed the Calcutta Convention, compelling the Dalai Lama's government to recognize the earlier frontier definition. Post-Independence –
Sikkim chose not to immediately join the Indian Union, maintaining its distinct monarchical identity under the Standstill Agreement.
Under the Indo-Sikkim Treaty of 1950, Sikkim became an Indian "protectorate," retaining autonomy in internal affairs while India took control of its defense, external relations, and communications.
This treaty allowed India to station troops in Sikkim and take any measures necessary for the defense of Sikkim or India.
By the early 1970s, demand arose within Sikkim for democratic reforms and closer ties with India, with the Nepali-majority population seeking greater representation.
Anti-monarchy protests grew in 1973, culminating in thousands of protesters surrounding the royal palace, forcing the Chogyal to request Indian assistance.
A tripartite agreement was signed in 1973 between the Chogyal, the Indian government, and three major political parties to introduce political reforms and hold fresh elections.

In September 1974, the Indian Parliament passed the 35th Constitutional Amendment Act, giving Sikkim the unique status of an "Associate State" of India, a position not granted to any other state before or since.
Under this amendment, Sikkim was not part of the territory of India but was associated with the Union, with provisions for representation in Parliament through nominated members.
This status was widely criticized as incomplete, and it lasted for only eight to nine months before full statehood was pursued.
In April 1975, newly elected Chief Minister Kazi Dorji appealed to the Indian Parliament for full integration, prompting a special referendum in Sikkim to gauge public sentiment.
A staggering 97.55% of the voters (59,637 out of 61,133 cast) voted to abolish the monarchy and merge with India, with only 1,496 opposing the move.
The referendum had a voter turnout of over 63% among eligible voters, providing a democratic mandate for ending the 333-year-old monarchy.
Following the referendum, the 36th Constitutional Amendment Act was passed by Parliament, making Sikkim the 22nd state of the Indian Union on May 16, 1975.
The amendment extended Sikkim one seat in the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) and one seat in the Lok Sabha (House of the People).
The Act formally abolished the position of the Chogyal and recognized Sikkim as a full-fledged state in the First Schedule of the Constitution.
To protect Sikkim's unique identity, Article 371F was inserted into the Constitution, granting the state special provisions that preserve its old laws and land rights.
It ensures that land and properties cannot be easily purchased by non-Sikkimese individuals, safeguarding the indigenous demographic and cultural character of the state.
Only descendants of Sikkim subjects named in the 1961 register are recognized as "Sikkimese" for land ownership and state government jobs.
Sikkim holds the unique distinction of being the only state in India where eligible native residents are exempt from income tax under the Constitution and Income Tax Act.
This privilege is secured by Article 371F of the Constitution and Section 10(26AAA) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, granted as part of the 1975 merger treaty.
The exemption applies to all income earned from any source within the state, regardless of how much the Sikkimese individual earns annually. Geography and other Facts –
In 2016, Sikkim was declared the world's first 100% organic state, achieving this milestone by completely phasing out chemical fertilizers and pesticides.
The state eliminated chemical inputs on over 75,000 hectares of agricultural land, transitioning more than 66,000 farming families to organic practices.
This sustainable model has prevented groundwater contamination, protected local biodiversity (including vital pollinators), and restored soil health across the state.
In 2018, Sikkim won the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) Future Policy Gold Award, dubbed the "Oscar for best policies" for its agriculture transformation.
The global recognition proved that a large-scale transition to organic farming is both ecologically vital and economically viable, setting a template for other Indian states.
The "Sikkimese Premium" from organic certification allows local farmers to fetch higher prices in domestic and international markets, improving rural livelihoods.
Sikkim is situated in the eastern Himalayas, covering only 0.2% of India's geographical area but holding immense strategic importance due to its location and topography.
It is home to Mount Kanchenjunga, which at 8,586 meters (28,169 ft) is India's highest peak and the world's third-highest mountain.
The state's topography varies dramatically, from the southern foothills at just 221 meters to the icy summit of Kanchenjunga, creating diverse climatic zones and unique ecosystems.
Khangchendzonga National Park (KNP) was inscribed as India's first "Mixed World Heritage Site" by UNESCO in 2016, recognized for both its natural beauty and cultural significance.
The park covers 1,784 square kilometers, encompassing subtropical forests, 280 glaciers, dozens of lofty peaks, lakes and waterfalls.
Located within a global biodiversity hotspot, it supports 1,580 species of vascular plants and nearly half of India's bird diversity, plus rare mammals like the snow leopard and red panda.
Sikkim borders China (Tibet) to the north/northeast, Bhutan to the southeast, Nepal to the west, and West Bengal to the south.

Key strategic mountain passes facilitating border transit and trade include Nathu La Pass (vital link between India and Tibet for centuries and was reopened in 2006) ,La Jelep La, Dongkha La, and Chiwabhanjang Pass.
China only gave de facto recognition to Sikkim’s integration with India in 2003, after decades of refusing to accept the merger as legitimate.
The state is primarily drained by the Teesta River, a vital tributary of the Brahmaputra, along with its tributaries like Rangit, Lhonak, and Talung.
The sharing of Teesta river waters remains a major contentious diplomatic issue between India and Bangladesh, with Sikkim's dams impacting lean seasonal flows downstream.
The Zemu Glacier (the largest glacier in the Eastern Himalayas) and the Lhonak Glacier are crucial formations feeding these river systems, critical for regional hydrology.
Despite its small size, Sikkim is globally recognized as a core component of the Eastern Himalayas Biodiversity Hotspot, hosting an extraordinary concentration of endemic species.
The state's vegetation is famous for Rhododendrons (over 35 species) and Oaks, while its fauna includes the Red Panda (State Animal), Tibetan antelope, Blue Sheep, and Gorals.
Important protected areas include the Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary and Varsey Rhododendron Wildlife Sanctuary, crucial for conservation of rare Himalayan flora and fauna.
The present population of Sikkim is composed of different races and ethnic groups: the Lepchas (the indigenous people), the Bhutias, the Nepali-speaking Indian Gorkhas (majority), and the Plainsmen.
Nepali is the most common language (lingua franca), with English being the official language of administration and education; Sikkimese (Bhutia) and Lepcha are also spoken.
The Bhutia and Lepcha communities are listed as Scheduled Tribes by the Government of India, a recognition that grants them specific constitutional protections.
On May 1, 2026, CJI Justice Surya Kant declared Sikkim as India’s first paperless judiciary at the National Conclave on Technology and Judicial Education held in Gangtok.

A fully paperless judiciary means all court processes — from filing cases to case hearings, evidence submission, judgment delivery, and record keeping — are done electronically without any physical paper files.
The system includes e-filing, virtual case management, digitized archives, and automated workflows for the High Court and all district courts of Sikkim.

topics.title: SCO Defense Ministers’ Meet
bullets: The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Defense Ministers’ Meeting was held in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on April 28, 2026.
Defense Minister Rajnath Singh led the Indian delegation, calling for a unified front to tackle the “evils” of terrorism, separatism and extremism.
The meeting concluded with member states reaffirming their commitment to strengthening strategic communication and advancing pragmatic cooperation to maintain regional peace. Background –
SCO was established on June 15, 2001, at a summit in Shanghai by the presidents of Russia, China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.
It was founded to strengthen mutual trust, promote regional security, and counter the “Three Evils” – terrorism, separatism, and extremism.
Headquarters - Beijing, China
The SCO currently has 10 full member states: India, Russia, China, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Iran (joined 2023) and Belarus (joined 2024).
It also has 2 observer states – Afghanistan and Mongolia – and 14 dialogue partners, including Turkey, Sri Lanka, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE.

The SCO is based on the “Shanghai Spirit” – a set of principles that includes mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, mutual consultation, respect for cultural diversity and pursuit of common development.

The Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) was established on June 7, 2002, as a permanent organ of the SCO to coordinate counter- terrorism, counter-separatism and counter-extremism efforts among member states.

RATS facilitates intelligence sharing, joint counter-terrorist exercises, extradition arrangements, and coordinated operations against terrorist networks, illegal migration, and trafficking in drugs, weapons, and explosives.
It has its permanent Executive Committee headquarters in Tashkent, Uzbekistan. The 25th SCO Summit (Tianjin, 2025) –
The 25th meeting of the SCO Council of Heads of State was held under China’s chairmanship in Tianjin on September 1, 2025.
For the first time, the summit took the form of an ‘SCO Plus’ meeting, expanding dialogue with observer states and international partners to address multilateralism and global governance.

It was attended by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and all heads of member states, and resulted in the adoption of 24 key documents, including the landmark Tianjin Declaration and the SCO Development Strategy until 2035.
The Tianjin Declaration strongly condemned the Pahalgam terror attack (April 22, 2025), marking a long-awaited acknowledgment by the bloc of cross-border terrorism.
It called for a unified fight against terrorism, separatism and extremism, stressing that “double standards in the fight against terrorism are unacceptable”.

It also called for the creation of a Universal Centre for Countering Challenges and Threats and an Anti-Drug Centre, and supported comprehensive reform of the United Nations to reflect modern political realities.
India joined the SCO as a full member in 2017 after over a decade as an observer, and became the chair of the Council of Heads of State from 2022 to 2023.

During India’s presidency, the joint statement of the Heads of State on “Countering Radicalization leading to Terrorism, Separatism and Extremism” was issued, symbolizing the shared commitment of all members.
India’s strategic influence was further expanded with the formal induction of Iran as a full member state during its presidency in 2023.
During its chairmanship from September 2022 to July 2023, India promoted the SECURE framework (Security, Economic, Connectivity, Unity, Respect, Environment) for SCO cooperation.
On April 22, 2026, the Indian flag was raised for the first time at the SCO Secretariat in Beijing during a special ceremony.
Secretary (West) Sibi George has also reviewed cooperation within the SCO framework with other member states to strengthen security, trade, connectivity and people-to-people ties.
India and China held their first SCO Bilateral Consultations in New Delhi (April 16-17, 2026) to discuss implementation of SCO Leaders’ decisions and the future course of the organization.
The two sides agreed to continue and consolidate mutual cooperation and consultations in SCO matters, reflecting a reset in ties following the resolution of border issues in eastern Ladakh.

The consultations were led by Ambassador Alok A. Dimri and his Chinese counterpart Ambassador Yan Wenbin, and focus areas included security, trade, connectivity, and people-to-people ties. Recent Meeting –
Rajnath Singh held bilateral talks with defense ministers of Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Belarus, focusing on training, capacity-building and humanitarian assistance.
Key outcomes included gifting two indigenous “Bhishm” Arogya Maitri Health Cubes to Kyrgyzstan and completing a computer systems and wargaming software project for its military.
These cubes are portable modular disaster hospitals that can be transported by air, land or sea and set up as mini-ICUs and surgical centers at any location within minutes.
Addressing the meeting, Rajnath Singh said the primary crisis today is not a “non-existent order” but a tendency to question the established rule-based world order.
He questioned the need for a “new world order,” advocating instead for an orderly world where “co-existence, co-habitation and compassion take precedence over chaos, competition and conflict”.
Invoking Mahatma Gandhi, he said “an eye for an eye makes everyone blind” and that it is the duty of Defense ministers to ensure the world does not descend into an era of violence and war.
He met with Chinese Defense Minister Admiral Dong Jun in Bishkek to discuss maintaining peace and tranquility along the Line of Actual Control (LAC).
The two leaders also exchanged views on the evolving regional and global security landscape, especially the developments in West Asia.
This meeting came after the October 2024 disengagement pact for Depsang and Demchok, marking a tentative but crucial step towards normalizing military ties between the two countries.
He also met Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov to discuss ongoing defense acquisition projects, including the supply of S-400 air defense missile systems.
India signed a $5 billion deal with Russia for five S-400 units in 2018, of which three have been delivered. A fresh procurement of five additional units was recently cleared by New Delhi.
The discussions signal the continued strategic importance of the India-Russia defense partnership, even amid global geopolitical shifts and India’s growing defense ties with the West.

Chinese Defense Minister Admiral Dong Jun called for the SCO to resolutely work together to improve security governance, eliminate the root causes of turbulence and conflict, and contribute to achieving sustainable peace.

He noted that the four global initiatives proposed by China – Global Development, Global Security, Global Civilization and Global Governance – have “injected precious stability” into a turbulent world.
The Chinese side also advocated for deepening defense and security cooperation within the SCO to drive the organization toward higher- quality development on its 25th anniversary.
The Bishkek meeting reinforced that the current era “should not be an era of war,” with Defense leaders upholding brotherhood and harmony.
By forging a unified front on a rule-based order and zero tolerance for terrorism, the SCO is emerging as a key pillar of global security governance alongside the UN.

India’s engagement — from its 2023 chairmanship to the 2026 Defense Ministers’ Meet, has strengthened its position as a responsible global power committed to peace and the vision of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam. The meeting highlighted the importance of multilateral engagement in addressing evolving security challenges, including terrorism, extremism, and regional instability. The SCO, founded in _______, includes major Eurasian countries and plays a key role in regional cooperation. Defence ministers’ meetings are a regular feature of the organisation, focusing on security coordination and strategic dialogue.
